entries.note: A hype cycle’s “slow, painful collapse” has no shared evidentiary threshold.
The claim attributes a collective private intention, rather than merely asserting market concentration.

entries.test: Public LLM training and operating costs, company financing, and evidence of market entry would establish whether resource requirements prevent most companies from competing at scale.
entries.note: The resource barrier has a plain economic reading despite the absence of a numerical scale threshold.

entries.test: Public financing and infrastructure records showing a private startup building and scaling an LLM independently of Google, Amazon, and Microsoft would refute the universal claim.
entries.note: The proposition faithfully extracts the sentence’s first assertion.

entries.test: Once LLMs demonstrate useful applications, public product ownership and infrastructure dependencies would show whether every LLM product is effectively controlled by Google, Amazon, or Microsoft.
entries.note: The prediction is universal and has no deadline.
“Minimal utility” and “minimal value” express an overall appraisal without a specified standard of worth.

entries.test: If generative AI becomes useful and enduring, public payment arrangements and infrastructure dependencies would show whether a handful of big tech firms take a cut from every LLM app and service.
entries.note: The normalized antecedent reduces the alternative to merely not being a fad; the context also concerns AI becoming useful and valuable.
“Well-positioned” to become “tech’s next landlord” supplies no agreed threshold for position or dominance.

entries.test: Public financial results, market concentration, and customer dependence would show whether generative AI losses and insufficient cost-justifying applications prevented the described oligopoly from taking hold.
entries.note: The normalization drops “I don’t think” and omits the second stated explanation: failure to solve problems that justify the costs.

entries.test: Public generative AI revenue and loss figures, together with documented deployments and their costs and benefits as of August 2024, would test both assertions.
entries.note: The claim has a plain financial and practical reading, even though comprehensive accounts may be unavailable.
He endorses this as a hypothesis about the companies’ private goal. The substantive claim concerns that goal, not merely whether he voiced the hypothesis.

entries.test: Public data on AI data-center capacity, specialized GPU ownership and procurement, and independent providers’ access would establish whether the four companies collectively monopolize this infrastructure.
entries.note: Market control and access are empirically assessable.

entries.test: Public evidence of AI platform control, business returns, and the causes of any collapse would test whether inadequate returns are the only circumstance in which the described monopoly strategy fails.
entries.note: “Only falls apart when” makes inadequate returns necessary for failure; the normalization instead makes them sufficient.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures showing whether generative AI produces sustained incremental growth for the big tech companies would test the prediction.
entries.note: Despite its present-tense phrasing, the assertion concerns generative AI’s future ability to sustain growth.
“May not” states a possibility, even with a condition and a time horizon.
